title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). The experiment used a shared‑initial generation: both conditions reused the same generated candidate and the guarded GVR pipeline could invoke at most one repair call per task. Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call); execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d. Results: baseline 299/300 passes (0.9967), guarded 300/300 passes (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis (target effect 0.10, ≈80% power) was not supported: a ceiling baseline success rate and minimal repair engagement (repair invoked exactly once) made the preregistered detectable effect unattainable. We explain why the null result arises from these arithmetic and execution facts, explicitly identify how auditors can deterministically locate the single repair provider trace inside the archived raw results, disclose which preregistered secondary analyses were not produced, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for stronger future confirmatory tests.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and remediation. Prior work documents that LLMs can draft plausible device configuration fragments but frequently produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors; guarded pipelines that combine generation with deterministic verification and localized repair have been proposed to reduce misconfiguration risk. The community currently lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that pair explicit intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and sealed preregistration for confirmatory comparisons. To address this gap we preregistered and executed study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1: (1) a deterministic synthetic intent→configuration task bank, (2) a snapshot deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) that enforces required‑sequence and workflow constraints, and (3) a paired comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass generator using a shared‑initial candidate design. Our final preregistered research question was: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate), does GVR materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Surveys and reviews summarize rapidly growing literature on LLMs for NetOps and emphasize key operational challenges—hallucination, prompt injection, verification needs, and evaluation gaps [https://openalex.org/W4406137434, https://openalex.org/W4415071524, https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical studies demonstrate that out‑of‑the‑box LLMs can synthesize router configurations but often require verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness [https://openalex.org/W4388629193, 10.1145/3626111.3628194]. Prototype generate–validate–repair (GVR) and tool‑assisted prompting approaches can improve final correctness in focused datasets [https://openalex.org/W4404652946], but these demonstrations are dataset‑specific and limited in scale. Security analyses of prompt injection and adversarial prompts further motivate guarded architectures and deterministic validators in NetOps workflows [https://openalex.org/W4405181600, https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. Our study contributes a sealed, archived proof‑of‑concept benchmark and a confirmatory paired run that ties a deterministic validator to automated repair under a tightly specified retry and budget policy.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. We preregistered ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765) prior to execution. The confirmatory primary hypothesis H1 asserted that the GVR pipeline would yield a higher per‑task validator pass rate than the frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration fixed task generation, validator semantics, inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness treatment, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and a repair budget (≤1 automated repair call per failed candidate). The design used a shared‑initial generation to isolate repair value: each task produced one initial candidate that served both as the baseline single‑pass output and as the guarded pipeline's initial candidate; the guarded condition could invoke at most one repair call on validator failure (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Task bank and validator. A deterministic task generator produced 300 synthetic tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 each); tasks encode initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, difficulty labels, and a required_sequence that must appear in a valid candidate. The validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) implements full_intent_constraint_validation as a stateless snapshot checker: it parses candidate commands into canonical field operations, enforces required_sequence and workflow_policies (ordering, mutual‑exclusion, group constraints), preserves unspecified state when requested, computes the implied final_state, and returns a binary pass/fail with diagnostic violation codes and a validator trace. Model and orchestration. The declared model was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version/requested_model = "gpt-5-mini") executed via the hosted adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with provider = "openai_responses"; execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) records invocation settings (max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null). Analysis plan. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on N=300 paired binary outcomes. The preregistered inferential test is exact McNemar (two‑sided); a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) was also specified. Missingness and sensitivity treatments (complete_pair_primary and failure_as_zero sensitivity) were preregistered; the run completed with no missing or excluded pairs.
sections.results: Execution accounting. Authoritative execution manifest entries: started_at_utc = 2026-08-29T12:41:43.384097+00:00, completed_at_utc = 2026-08-29T13:07:38.995000+00:00, planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301, artifact_hash_count = 2108. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json) shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 301 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}, demonstrating the guarded repair stage executed exactly once. Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (0.9966667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (1.0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55): n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.01]. Interpretation of p and concordance. The exact McNemar p depends only on discordant pairs (n10,n01); with n10=1 and n01=0 the preregistered exact test yields p=1.0—this reflects the extreme scarcity of discordant observations rather than a numerical error. In this ceiling regime the paired bootstrap CI (reported above) provides a more informative summary of practical uncertainty than the p‑value alone. Repair engagement and deterministic lookup of the repair trace. The guarded repair stage executed exactly once (repair stage_count = 1). Auditors can deterministically retrieve the single repair provider trace and the associated discordant pair identifier by extracting the sole record in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) whose provider‑stage field == "repair"; that record contains the concrete pair_id field and the per‑call provider trace. The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json cross‑reference provider call indexing and permit deterministic lookup of that record inside execution/raw_results.jsonl. Representative per‑task validator traces. Representative scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json … task-000006-*.json) illustrate normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after traces, and validator.valid flags; these files demonstrate the validator’s enforcement of required_sequence patterns (examples: shutdown_configure_restore; make_before_break_uplink_switchover; paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). Secondary estimands and omitted preregistered analyses. The preregistration listed secondary estimands such as per_task_failure_rate_guarded, per_task_failure_rate_baseline, and effect_size_Cohen_h_equivalent_for_paired_proportions. The archived analysis_results show secondary_results = [] (no secondary artifacts were produced). Because the run produced near‑ceiling margins (baseline ≈0.9967, only one discordant pair) the preregistered secondary estimand computations were not informative in practice and no secondary artifacts were archived; we therefore disclose that these preregistered secondary analyses were not executed to completion and note the consequence that effect‑size summaries beyond the paired difference (e.g., Cohen‑h equivalents) are not reported for this run.
sections.discussion: Scope and causes of the null/ceiling finding. The confirmatory null pertains strictly to the sealed design: synthetic intent→configuration tasks, a snapshot deterministic validator, shared‑initial generation, and a repair budget limited to one automated invocation. Under these constraints the guarded GVR pipeline rarely differed from the baseline because the initial generator satisfied the validator in 299/300 tasks; consequently the guarded pipeline could offer only marginal improvement. The preregistered target effect (0.10 absolute increase) was arithmetically unattainable given the observed baseline margin: the maximum possible paired gain with the observed margins is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 (the observed difference). Practical recommendations grounded in artifacts. The archived artifacts support explicit, implementable modifications to make repair efficacy measurable in future runs: (A) increase task difficulty or inject adversarial seeds to raise initial failure rates (execution logs show 299/300 initial successes); (B) permit iterative repair budgets per failed candidate (the execution provider audit shows repair=1 here); (C) allow multiple independent initial generations per task to evaluate selection/reranking rather than repair-only value; (D) adopt stateful/emulation validators that model ordered side effects and temporal constraints to expose execution‑time race and ordering failures; (E) include explicit adversarial test cases to exercise prompt‑injection defenses. Each recommendation maps to observed execution facts and to per‑task diagnostics archived in the bundle. Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design controls generator variance but does not evaluate multi‑sample baselines or selection strategies; the single repair engagement impairs contrast power. Construct validity: the validator enforces snapshot intent constraints but omits vendor CLI idiosyncrasies and asynchronous side effects. External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor) and we evaluated only gpt-5-mini and validator v5.0; results do not generalize to production networks or other models without further experiments. Conclusion validity: the small number of discordant outcomes (n10=1) leaves subgroup and failure‑mode inference underpowered.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR would produce a materially higher pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported; this outcome is explained by a ceiling baseline and minimal repair engagement (stage_counts record shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1). We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable the community to extend the benchmark with harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, multi‑generation baselines, and multi‑model comparisons that can demonstrate when generate–validate–repair pipelines yield measurable operational value.

Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implementing scoring rule "full_intent_constraint_validation"; per‑task scorer outputs and validator traces are archived under execution/scoring/*.json. Preregistered analysis executor: paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar and paired bootstrap CI; bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}. limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d).

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and execution/raw_results.jsonl) and are authoritative for auditors.
